item.title: 🔵 Why process excellence will become the competitive advantage in the AI economy
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

The AI revolution is here, and enterprises everywhere are racing to deploy the latest tools, agents and models. Yet, the simple truth is that access to AI technology is no longer a competitive advantage. Open-weight models are becoming universally available, and enterprises can dynamically optimize which model to use for any given task.

If the technology itself is no longer the differentiator, what will separate the winners from the laggards? The answer will increasingly lie in the layers of context, control and support around those models – whether agents have sufficiently rich, accurate and timely information about how the business works, and the right guardrails to operate effectively within it.

For decades, enterprises have been told that data is their most strategic asset. This remains true, but I would argue that a well-described digital twin of an organization is itself a strategic dataset – a detailed understanding of how the business operates. item.title: 🟠 Over 1,500 npm packages exposed by Trusted Publishing validation flaw
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

A flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing mechanism could allow attackers to hijack legitimate software packages by reclaiming abandoned GitHub repository names, potentially exposing millions of package downloads to supply-chain attacks.

Researchers at Bloom Security identified more than 1500 potentially vulnerable npm packages, including security scanners, authentication tools, and cryptographic packages.

The vulnerability, dubbed SlugFest, came from npm’s reliance on human-readable GitHub repository names to verify trusted publishers rather than the repositories’ permanent numeric identifiers. This could allow an attacker to inherit a package’s publishing trust by claiming a repository name that its original owner had abandoned.

item.title: 🔵 Stop sending me engineers: what OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft misread about enterprise AI
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

The AI industry says enterprises can’t absorb AI. Its answer is to absorb it for them.

That’s not the same thing.

The engineer across the table knew the model cold. Not vendor-deck cold. He could tell me where it would break, what it would cost, and which benchmark numbers to ignore. One of the better technical minds who has ever sat in that chair.

Forty minutes in, I asked which of our problems he would point to first. He named a minor workflow one of my directors had mentioned that morning.

The easy read is that he didn’t know my business. True, and not very interesting. Here is the real issue: the people who sent him are making the exact mistake they are being paid to fix.

They’re not wrong about the problem

The frontier labs aren’t confused, and I want to be fair before I disagree.

item.title: 🟠 AI’s hidden choices — and why getting them right avoids lock-in
item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

The first wave of enterprise AI deployments was straightforward: a chat interface calling a model, wrapped around a few clear use cases. The next wave is driven by autonomous agents that maintain state, revisit context, call tools and act under real permissions. This means enterprise AI teams must design inference, compute and deployment so those agents stay affordable, governable and compliant.

CIOs are used to making hard calls whenever the computing paradigm shifts. The move to client/server, web-based services and the cloud all required bets on platforms and architectures that shaped IT for years. The shift to AI feels similar, but the choices are more complicated, harder to see and harder to come back from. And the decision most tech leaders focus on first — which model to use — matters less in the long run than a set of less obvious but critical choices.

Six months later, all 11 tools are still running. The new platform is now number 12.

I’ve seen variations of this throughout my career, from financial services to media to technology companies. At CME Group, I eventually gave myself an unofficial title: chief decommissioning officer. item.title: 🔵 The great AI pricing reset is coming. Are you ready?
item.description:

Per-token pricing has become the default commercial language of generative AI, and practically every budget conversation now happens in those terms (tokens consumed, tokens generated, cost per million tokens, etc., etc.).

The problem is that this model treats every AI interaction as a discrete transaction, separate from the infrastructure required to process it. Yes, tokens are a billing unit, but the work they represent also has a physical footprint in memory and storage, and as agentic AI drives context windows into the hundreds of thousands of tokens, that footprint has outgrown the GPU.

So why does this matter? Well, according to recent analysis published in Harvard Business Review (HBR), corporate AI is about to experience a massive “cost shock”, as vendors move away from unmetered or bundled AI features and begin passing on the cost of the infrastructure required to deliver them.

IT and security leaders are well-versed in the risks of unauthorized integrations, misconfigured tools and vendor compliance. Now, AI has introduced a separate and harder-to-detect problem.

Across every function, employees use provisioned AI tools to generate production-grade code, build automated workflows and deploy agents to support business processes. item.title: 🔵 Governed context: The key to scaling enterprise AI
item.description:

The AI revolution is experiencing some growing pains. Across industries, business leaders are confronting the same challenge: AI pilots dazzle, but they don’t scale. An agent that reasons brilliantly in the sandbox turns unreliable the moment it touches a real, regulated business process. As a result, Gartner projects that more than 40% of agentic AI initiatives will be cancelled by the end of 2027, driven by escalating costs and unclear business value.

Or they point to the need for more context because a model starved of the right enterprise data will never perform reliably in production. This week’s vulnerability affects ADC and Gateway when configured as a SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) identity provider (IdP); older versions are also vulnerable when configured as a SAML service provider (SP), Citrix said in an advisory about the vulnerability, which it is tracking as CVE-2026-107406.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) has introduced an open-source sandbox for AI agents that allows developers to restrict their actions based on previous behavior, seeking to address security risks as enterprises give autonomous systems greater access to applications and data.

The tool, called Strands Box, combines operating system-level isolation with policies that govern what agents can do. Released in developer preview on October 7 under the Apache 2.0 license, it currently supports Macs with Apple silicon processors running macOS 15 or later.

Strands Box uses Dogwood, an open-source policy language developed by AWS, and its accompanying evaluation engine to determine whether an agent should be permitted to perform an action. The engine can factor in an agent’s recorded activity across different tools, allowing a file read through a shell command, for example, to trigger restrictions on subsequent network requests.
